name: LG C5 OLED evo TV
amazonQuery: LG 65 inch OLED evo C5 4K TV
summary: The default OLED for most home theaters: perfect blacks, Dolby Vision, four HDMI 2.1 ports at 144 Hz and sizes from 42" to 83".
verdict:
The LG C5 OLED evo is the TV we would point most home theater buyers to first. Every pixel makes its own light, so blacks are truly black and there is no blooming around subtitles. It supports **Dolby Vision, HDR10 and HLG**, runs **webOS 25**, and all **four HDMI ports are HDMI 2.1** with 4K at up to **144 Hz** (see [HDMI 2.1](/glossary/hdmi-2-1/)).

Size it for your seat. A 65" screen is 56.7" wide, so a 40-degree viewing angle puts you about **6.5 ft** away and a 30-degree angle about **8.8 ft**. At 77" (67.1" wide), those figures become about 7.7 ft and 10.4 ft. Run your room through our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/). If you sit 10 ft or more from the screen, the 77" is the better buy.

Four HDMI 2.1 ports matter in a theater: one goes to a soundbar or receiver over **eARC** (see [eARC](/glossary/earc/)), leaving three full-bandwidth inputs for a console, a PC and a streamer. At 144 Hz, each frame lasts about 6.9 ms, which helps PC gaming feel smooth. The trade-off is brightness: in a sunny room, the step-up [LG G5 OLED evo TV](/gear/lg-g5-oled/) and [Samsung S95F OLED TV](/gear/samsung-s95f/) get noticeably brighter, and Mini LED sets like the [TCL QM8K QD-Mini LED TV](/gear/tcl-qm8k/) go brighter still. For a dim or dark room, the C5 is a top pick in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/).
bestFor: Dim and dark home theaters, movie fans and console or PC gamers
skipIf: Your room is very bright during the day and you watch mostly daytime TV
cons: Less bright than G5, S95F and Mini LED rivals

faqs.q: What size LG C5 should I buy for my room?
faqs.a: Work from your seating distance. At about 6.5 to 8.8 feet, a 65-inch C5 fills a 30 to 40-degree field of view. At about 7.7 to 10.4 feet, the 77-inch does. Most people who sit around 9 to 10 feet away end up happier with the larger size.

faqs.q: Is the LG C5 good for gaming?
faqs.a: Yes. All four HDMI ports support HDMI 2.1 with 4K at up to 144 Hz, plus variable refresh rate. Combined with OLED pixel response, it is one of the best gaming TVs at its price.

name: LG G5 OLED evo TV
amazonQuery: LG 65 inch OLED evo G5 TV
summary: LG's brightest OLED yet, with a four-stack RGB tandem panel, refresh up to 165 Hz and a slim gallery design, for theaters that want OLED with punch.
verdict:
The LG G5 OLED evo is LG's flagship and its biggest brightness jump in years. It uses a **Primary RGB Tandem** WOLED panel with four light-emitting layers, which independent reviews have measured as notably brighter than the [LG C5 OLED evo TV](/gear/lg-c5-oled/) while keeping perfect blacks. It supports **Dolby Vision, HDR10 and HLG**, has **four HDMI 2.1 ports**, refreshes at up to **165 Hz** on most sizes, and runs webOS 25.

Brightness is what you are paying for, so put it in context. A projector giving 60 foot-lamberts on screen delivers about 205 nits (1 fL is about 3.43 nits). A flagship OLED's HDR highlights run several times higher, which is why specular highlights such as sunlight on water look so convincing. The G5's extra headroom also makes daytime viewing easier than on the C5. See [HDR explained](/glossary/hdr/) for why peak brightness matters.

For sizing, a 65" G5 (56.7" wide) suits seats about **6.5–8.8 ft** away; a 77" (67.1" wide) about 7.7–10.4 ft; and the 83" (72.3" wide) about 8.3–11.2 ft. It is designed to hang flat on the wall, so check whether a stand is included in your region. Against the [Samsung S95F OLED TV](/gear/samsung-s95f/), the LG offers Dolby Vision while the Samsung has a matte anti-glare screen. Both are top picks in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/).
bestFor: Home theaters that want OLED blacks with the most HDR brightness LG offers
skipIf: You are on a budget, where the C5 delivers most of the experience for less

faqs.q: Is the LG G5 worth it over the C5?
faqs.a: If your room gets bright or you want the most HDR impact, yes. The G5 uses a four-stack panel that independent reviews show is noticeably brighter than the C5, and it refreshes up to 165 Hz. In a dark room, the C5 delivers most of the experience for much less.

faqs.q: LG G5 or Samsung S95F?
faqs.a: Both are top-tier OLEDs. The LG supports Dolby Vision and has a glossy screen that keeps blacks deep in dim rooms. The Samsung supports HDR10+ and uses a matte anti-glare finish that handles reflections better in bright rooms.

name: Samsung S90F OLED TV
summary: A strong-value OLED with up to 144 Hz gaming, four HDMI 2.1 ports and HDR10+, a direct rival to LG's C5 minus Dolby Vision.
verdict:
The Samsung S90F OLED is the C5's closest rival and often the better deal. It delivers OLED's perfect blacks, refreshes at up to **144 Hz**, has **four HDMI 2.1 ports**, and supports **HDR10, HDR10+ and HLG**. Samsung does not support Dolby Vision, so Dolby Vision streams and discs play in HDR10 instead.

One detail to know: most 55", 65" and 77" sets use Samsung Display's **QD-OLED** panels, prized for vivid color, but some sizes and batches use WOLED panels instead. Both look excellent, but if you want a specific panel type, check reviews for your size. Sizing maths is the same as any 16:9 set: a 65" (56.7" wide) suits seating about **6.5–8.8 ft** away, a 77" (67.1" wide) about **7.7–10.4 ft**. Try our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/) for your room.

In a theater setup, four HDMI 2.1 ports let you connect a receiver or soundbar over eARC and still have three 4K/120-capable inputs. At 144 Hz, each frame lasts about 6.9 ms, good for PC gaming. Brightness is similar to the [LG C5 OLED evo TV](/gear/lg-c5-oled/): fine for dim rooms, less punchy than the [Samsung S95F OLED TV](/gear/samsung-s95f/) in bright ones. If you own a Samsung soundbar, Q-Symphony integration is a bonus; see our [Samsung home theater review](/samsung-home-theater-review/). More picks in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/).

name: Samsung S95F OLED TV
summary: Samsung's flagship QD-OLED with a matte anti-glare screen, 165 Hz and very high brightness, the best OLED for bright rooms.
verdict:
The Samsung S95F OLED is the OLED for rooms that are not dark. Its **QD-OLED** panel uses Samsung's **Glare Free** matte finish, which scatters reflections from windows and lamps instead of mirroring them. Add very high brightness, a **165 Hz** refresh rate, **four HDMI 2.1 ports** and **HDR10+**, and it is one of the most capable TVs available.

Here is why the matte screen matters in a theater that doubles as a living room. On a glossy OLED, a lamp behind your seat shows as a bright spot on dark scenes; on the S95F it becomes a soft haze that is far easier to ignore. Brightness adds to that: a projector at 60 foot-lamberts gives about 205 nits, while flagship OLED HDR highlights run several times higher, so the S95F keeps punch even in daylight. See [HDR explained](/glossary/hdr/).

For sizing, a 65" (56.7" wide) suits seats about **6.5–8.8 ft** back, a 77" (67.1" wide) about 7.7–10.4 ft, and an 83" (72.3" wide) about 8.3–11.2 ft; check our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/). At 165 Hz each frame lasts about 6.1 ms. The trade-offs are price, no Dolby Vision, and a matte finish that can make blacks look a touch lifted under direct light. In a dark room, the [LG G5 OLED evo TV](/gear/lg-g5-oled/) is just as good. See our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/) and our [Samsung home theater review](/samsung-home-theater-review/).

name: Sony Bravia 8 II OLED TV
summary: A QD-OLED with Sony's excellent processing and natural, accurate color, the film lover's OLED, held back by only two HDMI 2.1 ports.
verdict:
The Sony Bravia 8 II is the OLED for viewers who care most about **picture accuracy and processing**. It uses a **QD-OLED** panel, supports **Dolby Vision, HDR10 and HLG**, runs **Google TV**, and independent reviews praise its motion handling, upscaling and faithful color, which are Sony's strengths. It comes in 55" and 65" only.

The ports need planning in a theater. It has four HDMI inputs, but only **two are HDMI 2.1** with 4K/120, and one of those two is the **eARC** port (see [eARC](/glossary/earc/)). If your soundbar or receiver connects over eARC, that leaves **one** 4K/120 input for a console. With a receiver that has its own HDMI 2.1 inputs, route consoles through the receiver instead; see our [Sony home theater review](/sony-home-theater-review/) for pairing ideas.

Sizing caps out at 65", which is 56.7" wide. That suits seats about **6.5–8.8 ft** away (40 to 30 degrees); beyond about 9 ft, the image will feel small for a theater. Check with our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/). Refresh is 120 Hz rather than 144 Hz, which only matters to PC gamers. If you want a bigger screen, the [LG C5 OLED evo TV](/gear/lg-c5-oled/) and [Samsung S90F OLED TV](/gear/samsung-s90f/) go to 77" and 83"; if you want Sony processing at larger sizes, look at the [Sony Bravia 9 Mini LED TV](/gear/sony-bravia-9/). More in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/).
bestFor: Film lovers who want accurate color and top-tier processing at 55" or 65"
skipIf: You need more than two 4K/120 inputs or a screen larger than 65"

faqs.q: Is the Sony Bravia 8 II good for movies?
faqs.a: It is one of the best. Sony's processing, accurate color and QD-OLED panel make films look natural and detailed, and it supports Dolby Vision. It is less suited to multi-console gaming setups because of its limited HDMI 2.1 ports.

name: Sony Bravia 9 Mini LED TV
summary: Sony's flagship Mini LED with very high brightness and well-controlled blooming, for big-screen theaters with ambient light.
verdict:
The Sony Bravia 9 is Sony's brightest TV and its answer for big rooms with light. It is a **Mini LED** set with fine-grained local dimming, sold in **65", 75" and 85"**, supporting **Dolby Vision, HDR10 and HLG** on **Google TV**. Independent reviews widely note its very high brightness and how well Sony's processing controls blooming around bright objects.

Bigger sizes change the seating maths. A 75" screen is 65.4" wide, which suits seats about **7.5–10.2 ft** away; an 85" (74.1" wide) about **8.5–11.5 ft**. That is a realistic theater distance where a 65" OLED would feel small. Try our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/). Area grows fast too: an 85" screen has about 70% more area than a 65".

Like the [Sony Bravia 8 II OLED TV](/gear/sony-bravia-8-ii/), it has only **two HDMI 2.1 ports**, one shared with **eARC**, so a soundbar plus two consoles needs planning, or a receiver with its own HDMI 2.1 inputs. Refresh tops out at 120 Hz, and Mini LED will never match OLED's per-pixel blacks, though Sony gets closer than most. Against the cheaper [TCL QM8K QD-Mini LED TV](/gear/tcl-qm8k/), you pay for processing and refinement rather than raw brightness. For a bright living room theater with long seating distances, it is a top pick in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/).

skipIf: You watch in a dark room, where an OLED gives better blacks for similar money

name: TCL QM8K QD-Mini LED TV
amazonQuery: TCL 65 inch QM8K QD-Mini LED TV
summary: A very bright QD-Mini LED TV with up to 144 Hz and sizes to 98", offering flagship-class brightness for far less than Sony.
verdict:
The TCL QM8K is the brightness-per-dollar leader. It is a **QD-Mini LED** TV with thousands of local dimming zones, a 144 Hz panel, **Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+, HDR10 and HLG**, and **Google TV**. TCL claims **up to 5,000 nits** peak brightness, and independent reviews confirm it is among the brightest TVs available.

Put that number in theater terms. A projector delivering 60 foot-lamberts on screen gives about 205 nits (1 fL is about 3.43 nits), so even a fraction of the QM8K's claimed peak is many times brighter. That is why it handles sunny rooms and gives HDR highlights real impact. Sizes run **65", 75", 85" and 98"**; the 98" is 85.4" wide, which suits seats about **9.8–13.3 ft** away and covers about 28.5 sq ft, close to a 100" projector screen's 29.7 sq ft. Check our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/).

It has **two HDMI 2.1 ports** (plan around eARC if you add a soundbar or receiver; see [eARC](/glossary/earc/)). Mini LED cannot match OLED's per-pixel blacks, and some blooming is visible around bright objects on dark backgrounds, especially off-angle. Against the [Hisense U8QG Mini-LED TV](/gear/hisense-u8qg/), it is a close rival; against the [Sony Bravia 9 Mini LED TV](/gear/sony-bravia-9/), it is brighter for much less but less refined. See our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/).

faqs.q: Is a 98-inch TCL QM8K a projector replacement?

name: TCL QM7K QD-Mini LED TV
amazonQuery: TCL 65 inch QM7K QD-Mini LED TV
summary: A bright, affordable QD-Mini LED TV with Dolby Vision, HDR10+ and up to 144 Hz, the value pick for big screens.
verdict:
The TCL QM7K brings much of the QM8K's formula down to a lower price. It is a **QD-Mini LED** TV with local dimming, up to **144 Hz**, **Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+, HDR10 and HLG**, and **Google TV**, sold in sizes from 55" up to 98".

The value case is about size. Moving from 65" to 75" adds about 33% more screen area (from about 12.6 to 16.7 sq ft), and with the QM7K that step costs far less than with OLED. Seating maths for a 75" (65.4" wide): about **7.5 ft** for a 40-degree angle and **10.2 ft** for 30 degrees. For an 85" (74.1" wide), about 8.5–11.5 ft. Try our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/).

Expect fewer dimming zones and lower peak brightness than the [TCL QM8K QD-Mini LED TV](/gear/tcl-qm8k/), so blooming is more visible on dark scenes with bright objects, and off-angle viewing loses some contrast. It has two HDMI 2.1 ports, enough for a console and an eARC soundbar link with care (see [eARC](/glossary/earc/)). Compared with the [Hisense U75QG Mini-LED TV](/gear/hisense-u75qg/), it is a close rival at a similar price. For a family room or a theater where screen size matters more than perfect blacks, it is a strong value pick in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/).

name: Hisense U8QG Mini-LED TV
amazonQuery: Hisense 65 inch U8 Mini-LED TV U8QG
summary: A very bright Mini-LED TV with high refresh, Dolby Vision IQ and HDR10+, a TCL QM8K rival at a slightly lower price.
verdict:
The Hisense U8QG is Hisense's mainstream flagship Mini-LED TV. It combines high brightness, full-array local dimming, a high-refresh panel of up to **165 Hz**, **Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+, HDR10 and HLG**, and **Google TV**, in sizes from 55" to 100".

The 100" option deserves maths. It is 87.2" wide and covers about 29.7 sq ft, the same as a 100" projector screen, so it suits seats about **10–13.6 ft** away. Unlike a projector, it does not need a dark room or a screen. For a 65" (56.7" wide), aim for about 6.5–8.8 ft; for 75" (65.4" wide), about 7.5–10.2 ft. Try our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/).

Brightness is the U8QG's strength, and independent reviews rank it close to the [TCL QM8K QD-Mini LED TV](/gear/tcl-qm8k/). Like all Mini LED sets, it shows some blooming around bright objects on dark backgrounds, and contrast falls off at wide angles. Two HDMI 2.1 ports mean planning if you have a soundbar on eARC plus two consoles (see [eARC](/glossary/earc/)). At up to 165 Hz, each frame lasts about 6.1 ms, which helps PC gaming. If you want Mini LED brightness without Sony prices, it is a strong pick in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/); for a cheaper step down, see the [Hisense U75QG Mini-LED TV](/gear/hisense-u75qg/).
